Hi there! Thank you so much for reaching out. I’ve attached my mood board along with a couple of drafts I created with AI. For now, I need to stay firmly within a $200-350 price range, though there is definitely potential for additional work in the future as I grow and scale.

Thanks for sending the mood board and concepts. I really like the luxury, refined, and elevated direction you're pursuing. The budget is workable for me, and I'd be thrilled to develop a polished, custom brand identity that reflects your vision and helps distinguish your business. Could you tell me a little more about the brand, its target audience, and which elements from these references appeal to you most?

After spending months refining this direction, I have a few more thoughts that may be useful:

My most important realization is that the brand signature is no longer limited to the accent above the É—it now encompasses the full **V language**.

The larger opening V needs to serve as the wordmark’s hero. Both the smaller closing V and the É accent should originate from the same geometry, with all three sharing identical angles, proportions, and material language. Ideally, even if every other letter were hidden and only the two Vs and the accent remained visible, the result would still read unmistakably as VELLVÉ.

All of the other letters should play a supporting role rather than competing with the V. The most successful direction we identified was to approach those letters as architectural objects instead of conventional typography—restrained, sculptural, and deliberate.

I’d also love to investigate several further refinements:

• Adjusting the kerning until the word functions as a single cohesive mark instead of reading as "VE LL VÉ."
• Giving the Ls a more structural and less typographic character. We preferred taller, architectural proportions and understated custom geometry over ornamental serifs.
• Developing the É accent into a true brand signature rather than simple punctuation by making it slightly shorter, thicker, and more closely integrated with the V geometry.
• Testing restrained internal reveal lines or dimensional features that add depth without becoming ornamental. The logo should look capable of existing as an exquisitely made brass or stone sign whose details naturally catch the light.

Another key lesson was that pushing the architectural quality too far made the logo feel overly severe. I still want a timeless, sculptural result, but it also needs warmth, vitality, and aspiration. We discovered that this warmth came through material expression—champagne metal, light, subtle illumination, and depth—rather than through softer or more decorative letterforms.

You’re welcome to challenge the typography, provided the design language remains intact. My priority is to refine the wordmark’s DNA instead of introducing completely unrelated ideas.

In the end, I don’t see this as an exercise in making a beautiful font. The objective is a proprietary wordmark that appears inevitable, as if VELLVÉ could not possibly have been written in any other form.

Above all, I’d like the opening V to become distinctive enough over time to function independently as a long-term brand asset, without requiring a separate icon or monogram. The identity should reside in the wordmark itself.

I appreciate you providing these additional insights. This degree of clarity is extremely helpful and gives me a solid grasp of the brand's DNA. I understand that the goal is to strengthen and refine the established V language instead of bringing in new concepts. I'll treat the opening V as the central hero, maintain coherence throughout the V system, and work toward a timeless, proprietary wordmark that balances architectural structure with warmth. I'm looking forward to developing this direction and translating the vision into the final identity.
Thank you for the offer. I’ll begin working on your project immediately.

Could we concentrate solely on the identity’s foundation rather than producing complete logo concepts?

Because the opening V is the brand’s hero, I want to establish a unique design language for it before constructing the other letters around that foundation.

As we discussed previously, the defining signature extends beyond the accent over the É. It lies in the relationship among the larger opening V, the smaller closing V, and the É accent. All three should appear engineered from one shared geometry and should eventually be identifiable as VELLVÉ even on their own.

After that system is working, we can use it to construct the rest of the wordmark.

I’d also like you to move considerably farther from existing typefaces and pursue a fully custom result. It’s fine if the next round appears less visually finished, provided that it investigates stronger, more distinctive letter construction.

My sense is that once we solve the V, the remainder of the identity will develop naturally.

Hi [CLIENT_NAME_001],

Thank you for pulling back and studying the V on its own. I believe that is precisely the direction we should take. Before returning to the complete wordmark, I want to keep investigating the V because I think that is where the brand’s identity will be defined.

At this stage, everything should remain entirely black and white. Champagne metallic is still included in the long-term vision, but I don’t want color affecting our choices yet. Geometry needs to be resolved first. The material treatment should strengthen the design rather than determine it.

The V’s right arm needs significantly more investigation. Instead of reading as merely another letter stroke, it should become fundamental to the V’s construction. I want to test variations in its proportion, width, length, and termination so that it feels deliberate without turning decorative.

Its beauty must arise from proportion, geometry, and construction rather than from applied details. Each decision should appear structural, not stylistic.

We also need to keep the larger goal in view. If ELLVÉ were removed, the initial V should remain unmistakably identifiable as vellvé. That is the degree of distinction I want us to reach. When that is solved, I believe the rest of the wordmark will develop naturally.

Hi [FREELANCER_NAME_001],

To begin, THANK YOU for the tremendous amount of work you’re contributing. I sincerely value the thoughtfulness and range of exploration you’ve brought into this project. Watching the process grow increasingly disciplined with every round has been exciting.

The blueprint studies have been particularly helpful because they let me judge the foundational construction instead of focusing solely on the completed silhouette.

This round made it clear that the letter’s posture and overall proportions influence the result much more than its terminal details by themselves. Again and again, I responded more strongly to the letter’s overall construction and balance than to any single termination option.

I’ve also realized that the V’s identity will probably come from an overarching structural rule rather than one distinctive feature.

I want to keep examining a right arm governed by its own structural logic while remaining inseparable from the complete V. Its distinction should not depend on an overlap, joint, or any other isolated device. Instead, the entire right arm should seem to have been conceived differently from the left while still clearly belonging to the same letter. Any distinctive characteristic must feel required by the structure rather than selected for stylistic effect.

The left arm can be simplified further as well. I’d like to move even farther from classic Roman flares and toward a cleaner, more quietly resolved ending. In multiple studies, reducing those traditional references gave the right arm more room to carry the letter’s identity without becoming ornamental.

Something else I noticed while studying the blueprints is that the construction drawings often interested me more than the finished silhouettes. To me, that suggests we are very close to the fundamental idea, even though the final execution has not been completely resolved.

I see no need for new concepts right now. The opportunity lies in continuing to clarify the hero V’s structural philosophy until it appears inevitable. My intuition is that after the hero V is fully solved, the smaller V, the É accent, and eventually the complete wordmark will arise naturally from that geometry.

We’ve achieved incredible progress, and I’m eager to keep developing this direction.

Hi [CLIENT_NAME_001],

Thank you for such considered, grounding feedback. Your insight that the mark’s identity needs to arise from a governing structural law instead of separate stylistic devices is precisely the perspective a mark at this level requires.

I’ve worked on removing the remaining traces of traditional typographic language, reducing the left arm to its simplest form, and concentrating exclusively on the structural reasoning within the construction drawings that captured your attention.

For review, I’ve created two separate "Governing Structural Philosophy" systems while leaving all of the technical scaffolding fully visible:

The Dual-Axis System (Linear vs. Dynamic): In this framework, the left arm is a static, constant-width anchor. The right arm operates according to a separate mathematical progression, with its axis changing from a 2.0mm base to a 3.0mm top. This asymmetry is required structurally to counterbalance the lean and naturally produce the 48° inner clearing, with traditional flares removed altogether.

The Horizontal Termination Blueprint (Negative Space First): In this approach, the primary negative-space triangle is mapped before anything else and determines the letter’s entire character. The inner and outer edges are then calculated directly from that central framework, creating a completely flat, continuous, architectural top line.

Grounding the designs in these foundational rules makes the resulting forms seem inevitable rather than arbitrarily selected.

I'd like to hear which of the two structural philosophies you believe should become Vellvé’s definitive blueprint.

Hi [FREELANCER_NAME_001],

This is unquestionably the strongest option we’ve reached so far. The base no longer has a break, the right arm reads as one continuous structural form, and its perfectly straight inner edge finally causes the negative space to appear as a passive outcome rather than the central design goal. I believe you’re now approaching the challenge in the correct way.

Even so, it has not yet reached the degree of elegance I’m seeking.

The right arm remains overly bulky and visually weighty. I’m not looking for a clunky V or a "hero" right arm; I’m looking for an elegant V. At the moment, the right arm still attracts my attention before I can perceive the letter as a unified whole.

I don’t believe the answer is to make the right arm dramatically unlike the left. Instead, it needs greater refinement. Its strength should come through restraint, proportion, and precision rather than sheer mass. The asymmetry should register as sophisticated, not conspicuous.

We are also reaching a stage where the interaction between the two arms matters as much as the right arm in isolation. Please begin examining their connection at the vertex and how they can operate together as a single harmonious form with intentional asymmetry.

My ultimate aim is not to design a remarkable right arm. It is to design a remarkable V. The asymmetry must support the harmony of the full letter rather than becoming the defining feature by itself.

The right arm is not supposed to call attention to itself. The complete V should be resolved so harmoniously that its asymmetry feels entirely natural.

I’m looking forward to the direction this next refinement takes.

Leaving the heavy geometric blocks behind entirely, I’ve created three completely new directions centered on high-end luxury restraint, lightness, and the letterform’s natural harmony. Most importantly, every concept investigates a different sophisticated relationship at the vertex join:

Option 1: Intersecting Aperture: Two fine lines meet by crossing exactly at the baseline, producing a crisp, architectural intersection. The asymmetry feels effortless, allowing the viewer to perceive a clean "V" before anything else.

Option 2: Lapped Convergence: This direction uses a subtle layering principle. One arm settles gracefully onto the baseline, while the other rests seamlessly against it, establishing depth through proportion instead of mass.

Option 3: Merging Flow: The line weights stay beautifully balanced while gently curving and resolving into one continuous, fluid motion directly at the vertex.

The sheet includes close-up details of the vertices so you can examine how the forms interact naturally. I’m eager to hear which of these fresh and elegant directions resonates with you most.

Hi [FREELANCER_NAME_001],

Thank you for continuing this exploration. I believe this marks an important change in the thinking, and I appreciate that you’re no longer designing the right arm on its own but are considering how both arms relate to each other. That is absolutely the correct direction in my view.

However, I still don’t think we’ve uncovered the design language for this V.

Before narrowing toward a final direction, I’d actually like to step back once more and explore a much wider range of concepts rather than keep refining a single family of ideas.

Instead of showing several variations on one construction, I’d love to see fundamentally different interpretations of the letter. For example, possible avenues might include:

a V that is almost impossibly restrained
a V with a subtly sculptural quality
a V informed by the precision of stone carving
a V influenced by the elegance of an architectural cantilever
a V distinguished through optical balance rather than geometry
a V that builds tension through proportion instead of overlap
a V with asymmetry that remains nearly invisible until closely examined

the left arm’s quiet stability
the right arm’s unique expression
the relationship created as they resolve at the vertex

I don’t believe those elements can be solved separately.

confident
